items.title: From Context to Plasticity: A Three-Timescale Architecture for Persistent Memory and Recursive Online Learning
items.abstract: This work presents a theoretical architecture for continually adapting AI systems organized around three distinct timescales: (1) fast transformer key-value context for immediate interaction, (2) medium-term persistent recurrent memory with decaying importance and consolidation, and (3) slow, controlled parameter adaptation. The proposed pathway is context → persistent memory → importance estimation → consolidation → plasticity gating → bounded parameter update → changed future computation. The manuscript formalizes recurrent state dynamics, transformer attention, gated persistent memory, exponential importance decay, importance-biased retrieval, prediction loss, gated online updates, consolidation thresholds, and learned update rules. It also explains why adapting recurrent transition weights such as U changes state-transition dynamics, whereas updating memory changes stored state without necessarily changing the underlying transition rule. The package distinguishes inference-time state adaptation, memory adaptation, online parameter learning, meta-learning, recursive self-learning, and recursive self-improvement. It proposes controlled experiments comparing transformer, KV-context, persistent-memory, importance, consolidation, gated-update, and learned-update variants, with metrics for retention, transfer, forgetting, poisoning robustness, parameter drift, retrieval quality, and compute cost. This is a conceptual research architecture and falsifiable research hypothesis. It reports no experimental measurements and does not claim AGI, consciousness, human-level cognition, biological equivalence, or open-ended recursive self-improvement. items.title: From Context to Plasticity: A Three-Timescale Architecture for Persistent Memory and Recursive Online Learning
items.abstract: This work presents a theoretical architecture for continually adapting AI systems organized around three distinct timescales: (1) fast transformer key-value context for immediate interaction, (2) medium-term persistent recurrent memory with decaying importance and consolidation, and (3) slow, controlled parameter adaptation. The proposed pathway is context → persistent memory → importance estimation → consolidation → plasticity gating → bounded parameter update → changed future computation. The manuscript formalizes recurrent state dynamics, transformer attention, gated persistent memory, exponential importance decay, importance-biased retrieval, prediction loss, gated online updates, consolidation thresholds, and learned update rules. It also explains why adapting recurrent transition weights such as U changes state-transition dynamics, whereas updating memory changes stored state without necessarily changing the underlying transition rule. The package distinguishes inference-time state adaptation, memory adaptation, online parameter learning, meta-learning, recursive self-learning, and recursive self-improvement. It proposes controlled experiments comparing transformer, KV-context, persistent-memory, importance, consolidation, gated-update, and learned-update variants, with metrics for retention, transfer, forgetting, poisoning robustness, parameter drift, retrieval quality, and compute cost. This is a conceptual research architecture and falsifiable research hypothesis. It reports no experimental measurements and does not claim AGI, consciousness, human-level cognition, biological equivalence, or open-ended recursive self-improvement. The prefrontal-cortex comparison is functional only, referring to working-memory maintenance, goal persistence, error monitoring, and adaptive control. items.title: From digital libraries to future libraries: Reframing academic libraries as knowledge infrastructures in the age of artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the production, organization, dissemination, and use of knowledge. In this context, the traditional positioning of academic libraries as knowledge repositories is increasingly challenged by commercial AI platforms, while growing disintermediation raises questions about their role in contemporary knowledge ecosystems. Drawing on Infrastructure Studies and socio-technical systems theory, this study explores the conceptual transition of libraries from knowledge repositories to knowledge infrastructures. To support this argument, it proposes a “Four Pillars, Five Wings” framework, comprising four foundational capacities (AI model base, cross-media knowledge resources, full-chain knowledge services, and digital–physical integrated spaces) and five emerging capabilities (knowledge discovery, intelligent learning, collaborative creation, cultural activation, and research augmentation). Using Zhejiang University’s Future Library initiative as an empirical case, the study examines implementation pathways and discusses key challenges encountered during the early stages of development. The findings contribute to ongoing discussions on the transformation of academic libraries from resource-centered institutions into knowledge infrastructures in the age of artificial intelligence.
